11.3-p2: A retrospective feature published decades later in the News-Gazette, built on an interview with Joyce, fills in how the name reached Frank in the first place.
That article is used carefully here and in Chapter 13.

Its handling of the operational record is unreliable — it misstates where Frank formed his crew, inflates both his mission count and the aircraft’s, and describes him in 1944 as the father of two when his first son was two months old — and every such figure in this book comes from the orders and crew records instead.
What the article carries that nothing else does is Joyce’s own memory of things she was present for, and the committee’s correspondence, which she kept.
A widow’s account of what her husband told her about the day he landed is a different kind of evidence from a reporter’s grasp of how many missions he flew, and it is treated differently here.

The surplus from the bond drive was meant to buy a B-29 to carry the city’s name; the War Finance Committee, chaired by Ray S. Taylor, learned instead that a newly commissioned local pilot was forming a crew, and wrote to him directly.

The committee’s letter is quoted: “We learn from one of your brothers that you and your crew have completed all training and are awaiting assignment of a B-17.” Somebody, the letter went on, had suggested it would be wonderful if the city had one of its own boys piloting a ship bearing its name, “so it could watch the ship’s exploits with pride and hope and feel true community kinship with the pilot, ship and crew.” Frank agreed.
When the aircraft was delivered, the article states, he and the crew chose the name themselves — which is consistent with the nine missions they flew under it before the Army held its ceremony.

4.2-p2: A class yearbook for 44-D survives from this stretch, distinct from the Bainbridge class book cited later in this chapter, and Frank's own hand is on it.

Above a photograph of cadets tumbling off a train with their bags, he wrote "Welcome to Maxwell (Nuts)." Above a later photograph of the same men waving from a departing train, he wrote "Farewell to Maxwell (Thank God)." Between the two, the yearbook's own printed text describes the arrival — a haircut captioned "T.S. mister!," a retreat formation, cadets doubling across the parade ground — and the eventual transition to advanced training, where a cadet is treated as a pilot for the first time and the instructors as flight commanders rather than tormentors.
The yearbook’s printed text is stock class-book copy. His two captions are not.
The cover is dated September 1943: Preflight, Class of 44-D, Maxwell Field, Alabama, Vol. 3 No. 9, Paragon Press, Montgomery.
4.2-p6: A Kodachrome slide survives from the visit — color film, 1943, a small and by then increasingly rare extravagance. The collection’s own note ties it to what came nine months later: a son.
It is worth stating once, plainly, and leaving there. The photograph is already doing what it needs to do.
A second Kodachrome from the same trees names the other man Red Carpenter.
The book has no other paper on him.

2.1-p18: Sam Calicura Jr. was the field’s co-founder and its vice president. He taught his two younger brothers to fly there.
A group plate from the strip shows him fourth from the left, in a suit, no cap. The other men are not named here.

12.1-p2: Frank Calicura moved his cards into his that week — license, discharge papers to come, Joyce’s photograph, a stiff little card from a Soho club that could not be resold. He put the old wallet, worn soft against his thigh through twenty-eight missions, into the footlocker.
The tags that went with him still give the enlisted serial, 19149763, and Joyce as Mrs. J. B. Calicura at 731 Mellus Street. They sit on the same clipping.

13.1-p5: What happened to the aircraft on landing is recorded only in Joyce’s own account, given decades later.

Ray Taylor and other Martinez men had tried to reach Eighth Air Force commander Jimmy Doolittle through his peacetime employer, Shell Oil, hoping the ship could be brought somewhere townspeople could see her.
The War Department had other plans.
“The saddest part Frank said, was when he had to fly it back,” Joyce told the News-Gazette.
“When he landed, before he got his stuff off, they had dismantled it and towed it away.

He said if he had known, he would have gotten souvenirs.” By the time the Chamber of Commerce and the town’s service clubs held a luncheon at Armando’s to honor Frank and the other returning servicemen — a dollar twenty-five a plate, with a fountain pen presented to him in appreciation of the city’s obligation for naming his ship after it — the airplane the luncheon was partly about had already been broken up.
13.2-p2: This is a second correction, and it goes the other direction from the first one.
An earlier stage of the research assumed Sam Calicura Jr. died without seeing his brothers fly again. He did not.

A Gazette article from early 1946 records the Martinez Airport reopening under lease to Sam Calicura and Charlie Beatie, its landing-area designation obtained from the CAA the week before, with Ralph Donohue of Martinez — recently released from the Navy — as a third partner.
The field was limited to private fliers, with storage, repair, and a sales agency for a civilian airplane firm; no instruction this time, only operation.

Sam Calicura’s three brothers, the paper noted, would run it with him: Frank, a first lieutenant discharged from the Army Air Corps, doing what flying the field required; Nick, out of the Navy Air Corps, in charge of repair; Bill, who had served in the Navy air corps’ ground forces, assisting both.

That last description is the 1946 paper’s, and it does not match the wartime record set out in Chapter 4: an April 1944 Gazette item places Bill at Nashville, Tennessee, in the Army’s antiaircraft artillery, and his mother’s obituary that July calls him Corporal, a rank the Navy does not use.
Two documents written during the war disagree with one written after it.
The later paper is reproduced here as it stands, and the conflict is left open.
